Thank you to our talented MAD MAX: FURY ROAD crew for delivering spectacular visual effects, to George Miller for the opportunity to work on this epic movie and to everyone at Warner Bros Studios. MAD MAX: FURY ROAD noura. www.iloura.com.au Sydney | Melbourne

Dust, Grime, Sweat and Blood BY JOE FORDHAM he summer of 1982, Warner Bros. unleashed The Road Warrior onto North American cinema screens. The post-apocalyptic thriller (known in its native Australia as Mad Max 2) owed its origins to Mad Max, a 1979 grindhouse hit that introduced Max Rockatansky (Mel Gibson), former 'Main Force Patrol' police officer turned feral warrior — the first feature film of a former medical doctor.iI was working in emergency and I saw a lot of road accidents," explained director George Miller. "I'd grown up in Chinchilla, in the outback of Australia, where we had a strong car culture. We lost three of our school friends in car accidents. I confronted that in hospital, and I wondered how would that affect people dealing with that all the time?" Working with producer Byron Kennedy, Miller made Mad Max with limited resources. When I wrote the story for the first Mad Max, it was set in contemporary times. It was so low budget, we didn't have money to do car action in the middle of busy streets, so we set it a few years into the future, which meant we could use empty streets and cheaper locations. It was also an opportunity to make it a little bit more chaotici 1 / 28 The Road Warrior led Miller to direct a handful of well-crafted Hollywood films, in-

MAD MAX 4 cluding a third Road Warrior movie - Mad Max Beyond Thunderdome - that was touched by tragedy when Byron Kennedy died in a helicopter accident on a location scout. Miller dedicated Mad Max 3 to his friend and regrouped his creative energies in Australia, working under the Kennedy Miller banner, producing and occasionally directing an eclectic mix of dramas, thrillers and talking animal pictures. After two Babe films and a pair of Happy Feet animated penguin musicals, an idea for a new Mad Max emerged during a flight from Los Angeles to Sydney.iBy the time I landed, I realized I had to make this film," said Miller. "The story followed the Hitchcock dictum of a film that wouldn't require audiences in Japan to read the subtitles - it was essentially wordless, a continuous chase where people only spoke out of necessity and, in the helter-skelter of the story, we got to know the characters and their backstories. Miller teamed with graphic artist Brendan McCarthy to develop his idea directly into storyboards. "It was clear to me that this story was best rendered as images. Brendan is a brilliant artist, he was very familiar with Mad Max 2, and we developed the story with two other artists, Peter Pound and Mark Sexton, in 3,500 storyboarded panelsi Mad Max: Fury Road reintroduced Max (Tom Hardy) as he is captured by acolytes of Immortan Joe (Hugh heays-Byrne), megalomaniacal warlord of the Citadel, a desert fortress of 'War Boys' who control all water in the region. Max joins forces with the Immortan's lead Imperator, Furiosa (Charlize Theron), to kidnap the Immortan's harem of 'breeder' wives in a bid for freedom. Max, Furiosa and other beleaguered characters, including Nux (Nicholas Hoult), commandeer an armored War Rig, seeking a distant refuge 2 / 28 pursued by an armada of vehicles from the Citadel and other warring cultures.

Concepts quickly grew from Miller's visual story plan. "When I first walked into George's office in 2000," recalled production designer Colin Gibson, "the walls were filled with storyboards of trucks and warriors. At that time, there was no script, and I didn't design anything with drawings. I wrote a 'Bible of Tribal' that explained who the various tribes were and what their place was in this back-to-feudal society where all the fluids were running out - there was no fuel, no water, and even sperm counts were getting pretty low." A and some distant nuclear skirmish. Jump 45 years into the future, and everything from people's vehicles, to their weapons, even to their language is repurposed from found objects. Vehicles with microprocessors and crumple-zone technology are no longer useful. People go back to earlier technology, using vehicles from the '80s right back to the '40s. That influenced the look of everything. The Immortan's Citadel was envisaged as a desert settlement founded on an ancient mining camp.iThey have an aquifer, where they can pump their most precious commodity, which is water. Gold bullion, if they had it, would be useless unless they could use it to make bullets. And vehicles have assumed almost religious significance to the War Boys. They need fuel, which comes from Gas Town, a big fractionating installation. To protect that, there's the Bullet Farm in another fortress. Those three places formed the center of this treeless desert continent. MAD MAX 4 detailed backstory fleshed out world events. "The idea was 'the apocalypse starts next Wednesday," said George Miller. "All the bad stuff in our news today comes to pass - economic collapse, power grid collapse, oil wars, water wars, 3 / 28

MAD MAX 4 The production first searched for locations in Australia, home to previous Mad Max films, but Miller's desire to find more featureless, barren terrain led the production to Namibia in Africa. After prepping to shoot with Mel Gibson, slated to return as Max, the outbreak of the Gulf War caused the participating studio to grow nervous at a desert war fantasy, and they canceled production. The filmmakers mounted a second attempt at filming on the site of many Max Max 2 locales, in Broken Hill, Australia, and spent a year building vehicles and planning a new technical approach. "George and I were very much on the same page," commented visual effects supervisor Andrew Jackson. "We wanted to allow the randomness of real events to play out, to let live-action stunts and action run their course; visual effects would then paint out effects rigs and stunt equipment. Of course, financial issues played into negotiations. If a scene was expensive to do practically, the argument was why not do it as CG? My counter-argument was we could do the whole film as CG; but that was not what we were doing. We were making a film with the original Mad Max feeling, and that needed as much live-action as possible." To lay foundations for the desert car culture, the production constructed vehicles in a workshop in Sydney. "We built 137 vehicles representing 88 character vehicles," said Colin Gibson. ¿Each vehicle had a character and a story; and I worked with the stunt team and special effects department to make sure we all kept to the philosophy of the design. We went back to the glory days of the muscle car, with vehicles made out of heavy steel from Detroit, repurposed for battle." Head mechanic Mark McKinley gathered automotive salvage and four-wheel-drive mechanisms, but vehicle design remained a group 4 / 28 endeavor. We collaborated in deciding how we'd build each character car. Gas Town's

look, for instance, was beaten steel with a gas-rig mentality. They favored shiny, beaten metal, stripped back using what they had the most of: fuel. We worked out all those details together, and it became a double helix of design: one strand was what the movie needed for the story, the other was the internal logic of how we would achieve that.i To plan in-camera stunts, Miller turned to one of his long-time collaborators, stunt supervisor and action unit director Guy Norris, and special effects supervisor Dan Oliver, who together collaborated with the vehicle design process. Jackson and visual effects supervisor David Nelson, meanwhile, focused on developing previsualizations and, with CG artist Graham Olson, went on to lead an in-house team of effects artists - as 'FuryFX' - who shared work with the production's main visual effects provider, Iloura, and visual effects supervisor Tom Wood. finally returned to Namibia, where arid locations were a reliable commodity. In a public school house in Swakopmund, adjacent to the art department, makeup and hair designer Lesley Vanderwalt set up a team of artists to realize character designs that she had developed over the previous two years. A team of 28 artists oversaw makeup applications, handling prosthetics, makeup and hair with artists recruited from Australia, New Zealand and Africa. Prosthetic supervisor Damian Martin, co-founder of Odd Studio in Sydney, handled prosthetics creation. Another group, led by prosthetic artist Clinton MAD MAX 4 espite careful planning, unseasonable rainfall in Australia's New South Wales transformed barren wastelands into fields of green, causing the Broken fill location to become unusable. The filmmakers postponed shooting again and 5 / 28

MAD MAX 4 Aiden Smith, founder of Cosmesis Studio in Cape Town, South Africa, created photorealistic likeness dummies used in stunts too dangerous for live performers. "It was a big collaboration," Lesley Vanderwalt observed. "As Colin was designing the cars, that influenced our makeups. We started with the Immortan, who was covered in boils and scabies. To cover up his diseased skin, he'd covered himself in white clay in a ritualistic fashion. The War Boys emulated that look, and high-ranking warriors had more white powder on them. Bullet Farm guys were rusty and yellow from chemicals in weapons manufacture. Gas Town characters dealt with oil and fire, so they were dark and charred, covered in burns." Early in preproduction, Vanderwalt experimented with body makeup applications, and then developed applications for 300 performers. "Nik Dornin at Bluebird FX in Sydney made gallons of custom colors," said Vanderwalt. "We had a Citadel color, a Bullet Farm color, and a Gas Town color. As the actors came through, we shaved their heads, gave them a light coat of tattoo ink, and then we applied non-toxic clay mixed with powdered sunblock. Because of the numbers of extras we were handling, we only detailed ten key stunt people each day with prosthetics. The day before shooting, first assistant director P.J. Voeten, George and Guy decided which characters would come close to camera - it was a different ten almost every day - and they'd be the ones that went into prosthetics. Makeup details included mixtures of motor oil blended into warpaint to indicate rank in Imperator warriors, cancerous growths designating 'half-blood' and 'full-blood' social standing, and mutilations emblematic of automotive body art. We first thought 6 / 28 about giving everyone tattoos," Vanderwalt recalled. "By the time we came to shooting,

it seemed like tattoos were commonplace, so we settled on scarifications. Having worked with prosthetics in the desert, I knew dust always sticks to Pros-Aide applications. To avoid that, we used a silicone mold transfer technique that made the scarifications quick to apply, and worked very welli Martin and business partner Adam Johansen generated prosthetics using Polytek Platsil Gel-10 encapsulated silicone with Mouldlife Super Baldiez barriers. Soft translucent molds allowed makeup artists to align prosthetics to the performer's body and press appliances into place. a miser cat alone op foam with silicone skins. Likenesses were based on life-castings conducted at Cosmesis Studio and on location in Namibia, where Cosmesis head of engineering Adrian Smith oversaw dummy dressing and implementation, working with the makeup teams and wardrobe designer Jenny Beaven's costume team to kit out each body. The desert base camp accommodated approximately 1,000 crewmembers.iIt was a Western on wheels," observed Guy Norris. "It was like when John Ford would get together 40 riders and they'd spend three months filming in Colorado. We had 65 stunt people on location for nine months. On our biggest days, we had more than 150 stunt performers. We had our training base and gym in a factory in Walvis Bay, and when we rolled out to location it was like a military operation with different divisions - bikes, trucks and cars. Every morning I used a big whiteboard to brief the crew, drawing roadMAD MAX 4 he dummies team supplied 60 articulated performer likenesses. Hero dummies were cast in silicone over spring-loaded armatures, approximating human body weight and articulation. Lighter-weight dummies were cast in flexible 7 / 28

MAD MAX 4I maps and using Matchbox toys to show what we were going to do. ¿'On our biggest runs with the full armada, we had more than 100 vehicles. Everyone had radios with open coms. I'd sometimes communicate from a platform 30 feet in the air that looked out over the terrain. I operated a camera from up there, and called out events in a numbered choreography, like football plays. We had cameras everywhere, mounted on vehicles, with stunt performers operating cameras, as well as the main camera vehicles. George was out there in the middle of it, focusing on whatever section he wanted to cover as we went through the movesi Director of photography John Seale captured imagery primarily using the Arri Alexa M, four or more cameras shooting simultaneously, with smaller Olympus and Canon 5Ds in 'crash camera' situations. To aid dynamic coverage of action sequences, Miller favored the Edge Arm, a gyro-stabilized mobile camera crane engineered by Dean Bailey's Performance Filmworks. "The Edge Arm was like a three-headed brain," said George Miller. We had a very skilled stunt driver, a crane operator, and a camera operator remotely moving the camera. I sat next to the camera operator, Brooks Guyer, and watched the camera feed monitor, and the camera could go anywhere. We'd improvise in the moment, yelling out to each other as we captured scenes. It had a wild, immersive quality, and it lent a huge amount of energy to the movie. The Edge Arm's 360-degree pivoting head - capable of extending 23 feet from a four-wheel-drive Toyota Tundra - became a multipurpose camera platform. "It was completely self-contained and ready to go with very little prep," related Andrew Jackson. "It 8 / 28 was so valuable, they brought a second one out from the States. We used them not only

for their amazing ability to shoot driving action, but also as a dolly on static setups. Static setups involved 'Sim-Trav' scenes that emulated vehicle motion on stationary gimbal-mounted rigs. "The rule was, if the ground wasn't visible, we didn't drive the vehicles," said Jackson. "Occasionally, even if the ground was visible, we still didn't drive if a scene involved actions too complicated to do on the move." The production shot SimTrav scenes on location, taking cues from mobile scenes. We'd sometimes have one vehicle on a Sim-Trav rig, and then another vehicle rolled slowly by to create impressions of differential movement. During all of that, we kept the camera alive by maneuvering the Edge Arm, which drove slowly past. All those elements, moving independently of one another, were absolutely vital in keeping shots alivei We used big airbags, like those in truck suspensions, and combined them with hydraulics." As effects technicians manually jostled vehicles on the rig, unit floor effects supervisors Rob Heggie and Jabin Dickins wielded air movers to add airborne particulates, using approximately eight tons of non-toxic 'movie dust' to bombard performers. Furyfx artists Dan Bethell and Bodie Clare accompanied Jackson on set to capture environment surveys of Sim-Trav backgrounds.We often wouldn't bother placing greenscreens behind Sim-Trav scenes," said Andrew Jackson. "Sometimes it wasn't obvious if the sky, horizon or distant landscape were moving in relation to the foreground, as imMAD MAX 4 he special effects team built Sim-Trav gimbals as multipurpose rigs. George wanted a rig that could work quickly without a lot of computer programming because we were out in the desert in very harsh conditions, noted Dan Oliver. 9 / 28

MAD MAX 4 ages were so fast cut. George shot an enormous amount of footage, from multiple angles, and couldn't cover all those with specific backgrounds. So we grabbed a library of material, with a hierarchy of choices. We'd take the Edge Arm and shoot backgrounds at the height of the vehicle cabin, and then maybe a higher angle on top of the tanker. We'd drive up and down the location, shooting forward, three-quarter profile, and three-quarter reverse. That gave us footage to cut with any part of the driving scenes. We also gathered a library of high-rez environment stills that might be useful for CG builds. Iloura enhanced backgrounds to maintain continuity through traveling scenes. "Some Sim-Trav shots were more stable than mobile traveling shots," said Tom Wood. We destabilized those images to give more urgency to the camera motion. And we added dust, and animated wheels and lighting changes to help simulate the look of vehicles turning corners. There was a pick-up shoot at the end of 2013 in a dried up reservoir in West Sydney, and those scenes required removing trees, film crew and occasionally a car park. Most of the scenes were shot in Namibia with a flat horizon for 10 kilometers in all directions. We added undulating ground, dunes, canyons and hills, using various techniques. Occasionally, we built 3D environments derived from travel plates, and we created projections using textures from the Sim-Trav camera to get appropriate perspectives." The visual effects team also gathered location surveys using Sensefly Swinglet aerial drones and Agisoft Photoscan photogrammetry software that sampled digital images and built 3D replicas of environments. Photoscan images became a corner-post for a lot of our terrain studies and environment enhancements," explained Andrew Jackson. "They 10 / 28 very quickly gave us a basic model, and then with a little bit of work we turned those into

MAD MAX 4 renderable assets." The emphasis, however, remained on in-camera action. "We ended up with 2,600 shots in the film, and 2,000 of those involved visual effects. But I agree with what George has stated; this is not a visual effects film. We had 300 stunts, with a huge armada of vehicles in a real, gritty location. When you let all of that reality play out, you get stuff that you can't dream up." he film introduces Max on a desert mountaintop, where he idly captures and rubber lizard that the art department provided. Iloura animated the reptile skittering and meeting its demise. "We then painted out the lizard that Tom chewed," said Tom Wood.We emulated the translucency of the prop and enhanced the eyes and the 'spineyness' of the skin. We then animated the lizard's legs clawing at Max's lip, and its tail curling up." A gang of War Boys appears, causing Max to flee in a retrofitted MFP Interceptor — a battered version of the hero vehicle from Mad Max 2.iThe 1973 Ford Falcon XB Coupe was a place-marker to identify Max in this new world," stated Colin Gibson. "Max is captured almost in the opening beats of the film, and I thought that the War Boys wouldn't waste that classic car; and so, I suggested to George that we see Max's car after it has gone through this new world order. Later, the XB makes a reappearance in the hands of one of our villains, jacked up to four-wheel-drive, with a super-double-aspirated V8 and many more weapons. And then, Max is forced to destroy his own car." 11 / 28 The XB represented a poignant reunion for the stunt department. I was Mel Gib-

son's driving double on Mad Max 2," noted Guy Norris. "It was pretty interesting to sit in MAD MAX 4 the same vehicle, 30 years later. This time, I knew there'd be little chance of me performing any stunts as I was so busy, but I was very fortunate that they scheduled scenes with Max's car before the start of the main shoot. I did all the testing for the XB crash using our new flicker rig - a nitrogen ram that pushes the arm down and forces the car to flip - and because I'd done all that, I ended up the driver for that scene." Max recovers as prisoner in the Citadel. The production built Citadel interiors at Cape Town Film Studios, in South Africa, and shot exteriors at Potts Hill reservoir in Sydney. "We built an amphitheater area representing the base of the Citadel," said Colin Gibson. That included lower platforms and sections of the outer wall surrounding the base with three tiers of rock. Each tier held different levels of society, including 'The Wretched' - all they got out of the deal was shade and the occasional munificence of the Immortan dropping water." For scenes of Citadel inhabitants congregating for water rations, the special effects team rigged a waterfall in the Sydney set using pumps to supply several thousands of liters of water from off-camera tanks. Iloura added environment extensions. ¿We built what looked like three Monument Valley buttes," related Tom Wood. "The columns of rock protruded out of the desert around a plinth where Immortan Joe uses a ship's telegraph to release water. The special effects water sprayed down and splashed onto the crowd. As we developed our extensions, George asked us to make the water pipes bigger and increase the water flow. We did that using Houdini simulations with 16 layers of effects 12 / 28 passes to create water falling 80 meters." CG supervisor Clinton Downs created rock ex-

MAD MAX 4I tensions using scenic textures of Western Sydney's Blue Mountains projected onto geometry. Wide views featured 300 extras and motion capture animated characters that Iloura created to expand the crowd to 30,000. The Citadel crowd was pretty repressed. They were shuffling around, standing from sitting, sitting back down. When the Immortan appears, they cheer, raising their hands and waving water receptacles. We roto-animated those actions and replicated them as Massive agents along animated paths. n the Citadel, Max encounters Nux, a manic War Boy festooned with representations of motor parts. Makeup artists Elka Wardega and Brydie Stone applied Nux's makeup, which included clay appliqués and silicone-transfer scarring. The idea for Nux's scarifications came from a design I saw while Weta Workshop was doing some conceptual development for us," said Lesley Vanderwalt. "One of their guys who did costume prop designs had a small engine block tattoo on his arm. I took a photograph of that, showed the picture to George, and suggested putting a big V8 engine block on Nux's stomach. I studied books on car mechanics, and decided a universal joint would look good on Nux's arm, and a cog would look good on his hip. We dissected the human body into engine parts, and that's how we came up with a lot of the designs. After a failed attempt at escape, Max receives the Immortan's brand and a back full of tattoos that itemize his medical history as a potential 'blood-bag' resource. The makeup team created tattoo applications using custom transfers that Tinsley Transfers - prosthetic tattoo specialists in Chatsworth, California - supplied. Makeup artists Audrey 13 / 28 Doyle and Catherine Biggs applied Hardy's abrasions, scars, tattoos and hair design.

MAD MAX 4 Furiosa, the fiercest of the Immortan's Imperators, brutalizes Max wearing a mechanical hand on her severed left forearm. The production explored techniques for realizing Furiosa's arm as an in-camera effect. "Our first arm design was minimal," recalled Colin Gibson. George, being a man of great imagination, wanted Furiosa to be supercharged by her disability, and Weta Workshop came up with a beautiful design for a robotic super-arm. It was enormous and intricate, and it had to be operated by two people in green Lycra outfits. When Charlize Theron indicated a desire to streamline the appendage, the production compromised by using a largely practical approach that was minimally intrusive.iCharlize wore a shoulder unit and straps that supported a glove puppet. It was lightweight, and designed to look like it was built from found metal objects. We made a steel version, a lighter alloy version, and four or five super-lightweight versions. It could hold a gun, or dislodge an object from your eye. Visual effects added internal arm mechanisms. 'There was a gap in the arm between the wrist and elbow where Charlize wore a green sleeve," said Andrew Jackson. "We painted that out and added a CG steel shaft that created the illusion that her hand was mechanical. We had 276 arm removal shots, but they were relatively straightforward because the majority of the arm was present in the platei Both Iloura and FuryFX contributed Furiosa arm effects, including an Iloura scene in which Furiosa engages Max in hand-to-hand combat without her prosthesis. Charlize and her stunt double performed wearing a long green glove that extended about halfway up her forearm," said Tom Wood. "We replaced that with a stump grafted to her elbow. 14 / 28 Realistically, the muscles in her severed forearm would have been severed, or would

have withered away, but that was an unpleasant look and Furiosa had to be a sympathetic character. We had to ensure the scar on the end of her stump was not too gruesome, and we animated rotations of the bones to make the stump feel like part of her arm." inside the War Rig," noted Colin Gibson. "It was one of the more explicitly drawn vehicles that George and Peter Pound sketched in storyboards. We knew it had to be a huge offroad semi-trailer of enormous power that could hold up to 11 people in the cab, while hauling up to 40,000 liters of 'juice.' It was a Frankenstein monster welded together with a rakish tilt." The production built four War Rigs by cannibalizing 11 Czech Republic Tatra trucks, powered with laterally mounted pairs of V8 engines. One version was a breakaway that we could mount in different sections. Three we built complete; we could also shoot those as breakaways, and we could rig them for stunts. We built them all with real salvage. We were lucky to find a fertile period in the early to mid-1940s when the Chevy Fleetmaster was imported into Australia. We used quite a few of those as the hotrod shape for the front half of the rigi For closeups of performers driving the enormous vehicle, the production mounted the War Rig onto Sim-Trav rigs. A More Perfect Vision BY JODY DUNCAN n scope, story, and ambitions, Avengers: Age of Ultron is a big movie - even by the standards of Marvel Studios, which does 'big' as a matter of course. It is, in fact, the biggest movie ever produced by the studio, boasting a cunning android villain and the largerthan-life Avengers team: Iron Man (Robert Downey Jr.), Hulk (Mark Ruffalo), Captain America (Chris Evans), Thor (Chris Hemsworth), Black Widow (Scarlett Johansson) and Hawkeye (Jeremy Renner). The film also features nearly 3,000 visual effects shots, artfully crafted by 20 visual effects companies, all working under the guidance of visual effects supervisor Christopher Townsend and additional visual effects supervisor Geoffrey Baumann, with visual effects producers Ron Ames and Ryan Stafford wrangling the global assignment. "This is our biggest movie, in every way," said Marvel executive producer Victoria Alonso in the final weeks of postproduction.iWith so many visual effects shots and so many companies contributing, it took a massive effort to make sure everything was on track - and Chris, Geoff and the visual effects producers did a beautiful job of it." 1 / 36| The film, directed by Joss Whedon, also required an especially large-scale production,

Previs to guide the shoot was generated by The Third Floor, which came onto the project early on and stayed throughout production, contributing post-visualizations. Also on board at the outset was Industrial Light & Magic, which devoted much of its preproduction effort preparing to meet Christopher Townsend's challenge to take Hulk to a new, higher level of photorealism and performance. The opportunity to create the best Hulk yet was one of the reasons Townsend had accepted the Avengers: Age of Ultron assignment. "I had worked on Ang Lee's 2003 Hulk," said Townsend. "Then and now, Hulk is one of the most difficult characters to create. He's an oversized, bright green mutant caricature of a human being - now, make him look real. I wanted to take on that challenge, to create a Hulk that had a soul, that was more than just this beast who goes around smashing things. I wanted to make him so real that you would believe he was just another character in the ensemble, the same way you believe that Robert Downey Jr. is Tony Stark, and Scarlett Johansson is Natasha Romanoff. But, at the same time, we had to retain some of his comic book character; Joss was very passionate about that. He didn't want Hulk to be just a greenish, slightly bigger version of Mark Ruffalo. This Hulk would be an evolution of what we'd seen before. The prospect of creating a better Hulk was all the more daunting due to the fact that ILM had set the bar very high on the first Avengers. We've had several bites at the Hulk apple over the past few years," said ILM visual effects supervisor Ben Snow, "and, to my 2 / 36 mind, Hulk was quite successful in Avengers. That gave us a good starting place, but we

were keen to push it a lot further. AVENGERS: ULTRON As always, Hulk would be the product of art and technology - Mark Ruffalo's motion-captured performance, augmented and refined by ILM animators in a final CG character. The first part of that equation was aided by Imaginarium Studios, a performance capture company founded by actor Andy Serkis, whose expertise in the discipline had been honed in a series of Peter Jackson films. "Andy Serkis has a lot of experience playing these sorts of characters," noted Snow, "and he had developed techniques for owning a character, even in the mocap getup. For example, on King Kong, he had used a voice amplifier on set that allowed him to make very loud roars and grunts. So, for this film, he suggested that we hook up Mark Ruffalo with something similar, to enable him to sound like Hulk on stage. Another technique that assisted Ruffalo on set was real-time playback on monitors that showed, roughly, what his physical performance would look like in its final form.iWe used our face library from the first film to create what we called ILM's 'Monster Mirror,' which allowed Mark to see himself as Hulk as he performed," explained Snow. "It wasn't exactly what the final animation would be, but it was a good tool for getting Mark in a Hulk mood." Ruffalo also wore cricket gloves to make his hands larger, while a weighted vest and weights on his wrists and ankles simulated Hulk's gravitas and power. Ruffalo first explored his Hulk persona on Imaginarium's stages in London, then in a motion capture volume built at Shepperton Studios. The idea of a public bored with the attractions offered at the dinosaur theme park, the realization of entrepreneur John Hammond's dream, was at the core of Jurassic World's narrative, which has park owners so desperate to win back attendance that they create a new 'super' dinosaur, the Indominus rex, by combining the genetic material of a velociraptor with that of a T-rex.
